14430:
The single most important idea to hold onto: when something is described as septic, it means it is infected — or causes infection — specifically through harmful bacteria that rot, decay, or destroy what they invade.

Bacteria are everywhere. Most are harmless, many are beneficial. But certain bacteria, when they invade the wrong place — a wound, the bloodstream, a joint, living tissue — begin multiplying and breaking down whatever they touch. That process is called sepsis. The adjective septic describes anything that either is in that infected, bacterially overrun state or relates to or promotes that kind of bacterial breakdown.
The Medical Meaning (the most common use)

This is where you'll encounter the word most often, and it always carries a sense of danger.

When a wound is described as septic, it means harmful bacteria have invaded it and are actively destroying tissue. Picture a small cut on your hand that's left dirty and untreated. Bacteria enter it. The skin around it turns red, hot, and swollen. Pus begins to form. The wound has "gone septic." It's no longer just an injury — it's now an active site of bacterial infection and decay.

The word implies something worse than "dirty" or even just "infected." A septic condition is one where bacteria are multiplying, spreading, and breaking things down. Left untreated, it escalates.

Here are the most common septic phrases you'll see in a medical context:

A septic wound is a wound that has become infected with bacteria, usually showing swelling, redness, and pus — visible signs that bacteria are at work destroying tissue.

Septic shock is a severe, life-threatening emergency. It happens when bacteria (or the toxic substances they release) flood the bloodstream in large quantities, causing the body's blood pressure to crash and organs to begin failing. This is the extreme end of what "septic" can mean — a body-wide crisis.

Septic arthritis is when bacteria infect a joint — a knee, shoulder, or hip, for example. The joint becomes intensely painful, swollen, and hot. It's serious because bacteria inside a joint can destroy the cartilage quickly if not treated.

Septic conditions describes an environment or situation that is prone to promoting bacterial infection — like an unclean operating room, or unsanitary living conditions.

What unites all of these is the idea that bacteria are present, active, harmful, and in the process of breaking something down.

Understanding the opposite helps cement the meaning. Aseptic means completely free of harmful bacteria — sterile. Surgeons work in aseptic environments. Medical instruments are sterilized to make them aseptic. If septic means overrun with harmful bacteria, aseptic means the complete absence of them. The two words are mirror images.

There is a second, completely different context where "septic" appears, and it's much calmer — almost technical. This is the world of waste treatment.

A septic tank is an underground chamber, common in rural homes or areas without centralized sewage systems, where raw household sewage flows in and bacteria naturally decompose and break it down. Here, "septic" isn't a warning — it's a description of how the system functions. The bacteria are doing useful, intentional work.

A septic system refers to the broader network of pipes, tanks, and drainage fields that manages this bacterial decomposition process on a property.

In this context, septic means relating to the bacterial decomposition of organic waste. The decay is controlled, contained, and purposeful. There's no danger being described — just a process.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

When "septic" appears alongside medical words — wound, shock, arthritis, infection, blood — it means harmful bacterial infection. When it appears alongside words like tank, system, or drain field, it means bacterial waste decomposition. The context makes it clear every time.

No matter where you see the word, septic always has bacteria and decay at its center. In medicine, that decay is the enemy — something going wrong in the body. In waste systems, that decay is the tool — something working exactly as intended. The word describes the same biological process (bacteria breaking down organic matter), but whether that's dangerous or useful depends entirely on where it's happening and what is being broken down.
14431:
A septuagenarian is a person who is in their seventies — that is, someone who is at least 70 years old but has not yet reached their 80th birthday. If you know someone who is 70, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, or 79 years old, that person is a septuagenarian.

The exact boundaries: The word has very precise edges. A person becomes a septuagenarian the moment they turn 70. They stop being one the moment they turn 80. Not a day before, not a day after. So the word covers a strict ten-year window of a human life.

What the word does NOT mean: The word says nothing at all about the person's health, personality, energy level, wisdom, or lifestyle. A 76-year-old who runs marathons and a 76-year-old who rarely leaves the house are both, equally and without distinction, septuagenarians. The word is purely about age — nothing more.

The tone and register: Septuagenarian is a formal, slightly literary word. You are far more likely to encounter it in a newspaper article, an official biography, a medical report, or a formal speech than in ordinary conversation. In casual speech, people typically just say "she's in her seventies" or "he's a seventy-something." In writing, however, septuagenarian adds both precision and a certain elegance. It tells you not just roughly how old someone is, but pinpoints exactly which decade of their life they are in.

• "The prize was awarded to a determined septuagenarian who had spent her seventies learning five new languages."
  • "At 74, the retired judge remained one of the sharpest septuagenarians in the legal community."
  • "The study followed a group of 200 septuagenarians over a period of five years."

Notice in each sentence that "septuagenarian" works just like any other noun referring to a person — it can be the subject of a sentence, the object, or used in a group/plural form.

Its place in a family of similar words: English has a neat, logical set of words that work exactly the same way for other decades of later life. Knowing the whole family makes the meaning of septuagenarian stick much better:

A sexagenarian is someone in their sixties (60–69). A septuagenarian is someone in their seventies (70–79). An octogenarian is someone in their eighties (80–89). A nonagenarian is someone in their nineties (90–99). A centenarian is someone who is 100 years old or older.

You can see the clean pattern: each word names a specific ten-year stretch of later life. Septuagenarian sits right in the middle of this family.

One small bonus note — adjective use: It is worth knowing that the very same word can also sit in front of another noun to describe it, functioning as an adjective. For example: "a septuagenarian athlete" or "septuagenarian voters." The word does not change its spelling or form when it does this. This is worth knowing so that you are not confused when you encounter it used that way in the wild.

The one-sentence summary to remember forever: A septuagenarian is simply any person who is aged between 70 and 79 years old — no more, no less.
14432:
A septum is a thin wall or partition that divides a space into two separate sections. Think of it as an internal divider — like a fence that runs through the middle of a space to keep two sides separate from each other.

The word is used across many fields — anatomy, biology, and even lab science — but the idea is always the same: a septum separates two regions.
The Most Familiar Septum: The One in Your Nose

When most people hear the word "septum," they picture the nasal septum — and that's a great place to start.

Your nose has two nostrils, right? Well, there's a wall running down the middle of your nose that creates those two separate air passages. That wall is your nasal septum. It is made partly of cartilage (the flexible, rubbery tissue at the front of your nose) and partly of bone further back.

Its job is straightforward: it divides your nasal cavity into a left side and a right side, so air enters and flows through two distinct channels before reaching your throat and lungs.

Your heart also has septa (plural of septum — more on that below). The heart has four chambers — two on the left and two on the right. The wall separating the two upper chambers (called atria) is the interatrial septum. The wall separating the two lower chambers (called ventricles) is the interventricular septum.

These septa are critical because they keep oxygen-rich blood and oxygen-poor blood from mixing inside the heart. Without them, your heart couldn't function as an efficient pump.

The concept of a septum extends beyond the human body:

  • In fungi, the long thread-like strands (called hyphae) that make up the body of a fungus are often divided internally by cross-walls called septa. These walls separate the strand into individual cell-like units, though sometimes tiny pores in the septa still allow material to pass through.
  • In plant pods and fruits, septa are the internal membranes that divide the inside into compartments. For example, in a bell pepper, if you cut it open and see those white ridges separating the hollow sections, those ridge-walls are septa. Similarly, inside a pomegranate or a citrus fruit, the papery walls that separate the juicy segments are septa.

In chemistry and lab work, the word "septum" refers to something a little different: a rubber or silicone disc used to seal the opening of a bottle, vial, or flask. It's a tight, flexible seal that keeps whatever's inside contained — but crucially, it allows a needle or syringe to pierce through it to inject or withdraw a liquid without fully opening the container. This is vital for handling sensitive substances that shouldn't be exposed to air.

The plural of septum is septa (from its Latin origin, though you don't need the history). You might also occasionally see "septums" used in informal or everyday writing, and that's acceptable too — but septa is the standard, especially in scientific and medical contexts.

Deviated septum: This is when the nasal septum is not perfectly centered — it leans noticeably to one side. Many people have a mildly deviated septum and never notice it, but a significant deviation can block one nostril, make breathing difficult, cause snoring, or lead to frequent sinus problems. It can be corrected with surgery.

Perforated septum: This means there is a hole in the nasal septum. It can be caused by trauma, long-term cocaine use, certain infections, or medical conditions. A hole in the septum can cause whistling sounds when breathing, crusting, nosebleeds, or difficulty breathing.

Septum piercing: A popular body piercing done at the lower front of the nose. Despite the name, the piercing most commonly goes through the soft tissue just below the cartilaginous septum (not through the cartilage itself), because that spot is less painful and heals more easily. However, some piercings do go through the cartilage of the septum itself.

Open vs. closed septum (in fungi): Fungal septa can have pores that allow cytoplasm to pass between cells (called dolipore or simple septa, depending on the type of fungus), or they can be fully closed in certain organisms. This distinction matters in classifying types of fungi.
A Summary to Tie It All Together

A septum is simply a dividing wall or partition found inside a body, organism, or even a lab tool. Its purpose is always to separate two spaces or chambers from each other. In your nose, it splits your nasal cavity in two. In your heart, it keeps the two sides from mixing blood. In fungi and fruits, it divides structures into compartments. In a lab vial, it seals an opening while still allowing access via needle.

The word is versatile, but its meaning is consistent: wherever you see it, picture a thin dividing wall doing the work of keeping two things separate.
14433: A sepulcher is a tomb — a place where a dead person's body is placed and sealed, usually permanently. But it's not just any burial spot. A sepulcher is specifically a chamber or hollow space built or carved to hold a body, as opposed to a simple hole dug in the ground. Think of it as a room for the dead, often made of stone, either constructed above the ground or cut directly into a rock face or hillside.
How it differs from similar words

This is where learners often get fuzzy, so let's be precise.

A grave is the most basic form of burial — just a pit dug into the earth, the body placed in, and the earth covered back over it. Very simple, very common.

A tomb is a broader, more general word for any structure or place meant to house the dead. All sepulchers are tombs, but not all tombs are sepulchers.

A sepulcher is more specific: it is always enclosed — a chamber with walls, a ceiling, and usually a sealed entrance (like a heavy stone door or slab). It is almost always made of stone or rock, and it is typically the kind of burial reserved for someone of importance: a king, a religious figure, a nobleman. It has a sense of permanence, gravity, and weight to it — both literally and emotionally.

A mausoleum is a large, grand above-ground building erected specifically as a tomb (often for royalty or very wealthy families). A crypt is an underground chamber, usually beneath a church or cathedral, where the dead are kept. A sepulcher is older and rawer than a mausoleum, and it doesn't have to be underground like a crypt.

Picture a hillside in an ancient land. Someone has carved a rectangular chamber straight into the rock. The inside is bare stone — cool, dark, silent. There may be a stone ledge or shelf along the wall where the body is laid. The entrance is a low doorway, sealed shut with a large, heavy stone disc or slab. That is a sepulcher. It is not decorated like a palace. It is not grand like a cathedral. It is simply a stone room, carved into the earth or rock, for the purpose of holding a body away from the elements, animals, and the living world.
Famous examples that will help it click

The most famous sepulcher in the world is the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem — the site that Christians believe is the tomb of Jesus Christ, where his body was laid after the crucifixion and from which, according to Christian belief, he rose. This is a real, physical site that still exists today and has a church built over it. This one example alone tells you a great deal about the word: the Holy Sepulchre is an enclosed stone chamber, carved into rock, sealed with a stone, belonging to an enormously significant figure. That is precisely what a sepulcher is.

Ancient Egyptian burial chambers, the rock-cut tombs of Petra in Jordan, and the stone burial chambers found across the ancient Middle East and Mediterranean world are all sepulchers.

The word also appears in a powerful figurative phrase: "whited sepulcher" (or whitened sepulcher). This expression comes from the Bible, where Jesus criticizes certain religious leaders by saying they are like tombs that have been painted white on the outside — they look clean and beautiful — but inside, they are full of dead bones and rot.

So a "whited sepulcher" has come to mean a person or thing that appears righteous, honorable, and admirable on the outside, but is deeply corrupt, hollow, or morally rotten on the inside. The beauty is a disguise. The real interior is death.

This figurative use is quite powerful and you may encounter it in literature, speeches, or criticism even today.
The tone and feel of the word

Sepulcher is not a word you'd use in everyday casual conversation. It belongs to serious, solemn, or elevated contexts — religious writing, literature, historical accounts, poetry. When a writer chooses "sepulcher" instead of "tomb" or "grave," they are deliberately reaching for something weightier, more ancient-feeling, more permanent and solemn. The word carries an atmosphere of cold stone, silence, darkness, and finality. It is a word that feels like what it describes.

A sepulcher is an enclosed stone burial chamber — typically carved into rock or built of stone — where a body is placed and sealed. It is more enclosed and specific than a general tomb, more ancient and raw than a mausoleum, and carries a tone of permanence and solemnity. It appears most often in religious, historical, and literary contexts. Figuratively, a "whited sepulcher" describes something or someone that hides inner corruption behind an attractive outer appearance.
14434:
A sepulchre is a tomb — a stone chamber where a dead body is placed. Think of ancient burial vaults, underground crypts, or those cold stone rooms inside old churches where the dead lie. "Sepulchral" means of, relating to, or strongly suggesting a tomb and everything associated with it.

That "everything associated with it" is the key. When you call something sepulchral, you are saying it carries the qualities of a tomb: the deep hollow silence, the cold gloom, the heavy atmosphere of death. It is not just about literal tombs — it is about capturing the feeling of one.
The Two Ways It Is Used

1. The Literal Sense

Something is sepulchral if it directly belongs to, or is meant for, a tomb or burial.

The cemetery was filled with sepulchral monuments — stone arches, carved figures, and heavy iron crosses.

Here, "sepulchral" simply means funerary — designed for or associated with burial. This is the more straightforward, less commonly used sense.

2. The Figurative Sense (The Important One)

This is where the word does its real work. Something is called sepulchral when it evokes the atmosphere of a tomb — even if there is no actual tomb in sight. It is used to describe three kinds of things:

a) Voices and Sounds
A sepulchral voice is deep, hollow, slow, and gloomy — like a sound rising from the depths of a stone vault. It is not simply a deep voice. It has a particular deadness to it. An eerie, resonant hollowness. When a character in a story speaks in a sepulchral tone, you feel a chill — as if the words themselves came from somewhere underground.

"It is too late," he said in a sepulchral voice, barely above a whisper.

You can hear it, can't you? Slow. Heavy. Hollow. Almost inhuman.

b) Silence and Atmosphere
Sepulchral silence is not just quiet — it is the specific silence of a tomb. Oppressive. Total. So deep that it feels wrong. The kind of silence where you become acutely aware that something is missing — life, warmth, movement.

The abandoned hospital was sepulchral — cold corridors, not a sound, dust settled on everything like snow.

c) Appearance and Light
Something can look sepulchral if it has the visual quality of a tomb: dim, pale, gloomy, shadowed. A face bathed in cold grey light can look sepulchral. A room with no warmth in its light can feel sepulchral.

A single candle cast a sepulchral glow over the room, making every face look like a death mask.

To really lock this word in, understand that "sepulchral" is not a general word for "dark" or "sad" or "scary." It is very specific. It points to a particular combination of qualities:

  • Hollow — like sound or space that has emptied out
  • Cold — not physically cold necessarily, but emotionally and atmospherically cold
  • Still — an unnatural, heavy stillness
  • Gloomy — but a deep, weighty kind of gloom, not just sadness
  • Deathly — carrying a strong suggestion of mortality and the grave

If something is merely dark, call it dark. If something is merely sad, call it sad. But if it has that specific tomb-like quality — hollow, hushed, heavy with the presence of death — that is when "sepulchral" earns its place.

• It does not simply mean sad or mournful. A person crying at a funeral is mournful, not sepulchral. But the echoing stone hall of the funeral home is sepulchral.
  • It does not mean terrifying in a dramatic way. Sepulchral is quieter and more suffocating than dramatic terror.
  • It does not mean just dark or gloomy. A rainy Monday can be gloomy. A sepulchral scene has something specific and deathly about it that a rainy Monday does not.

Writers tend to pair "sepulchral" with specific nouns. Here are the most common ones, each showing how the word flexes across contexts:

  • Sepulchral voice / tone / whisper — a hollow, deep, death-tinged way of speaking
  • Sepulchral silence — a total, oppressive, tomb-like absence of sound
  • Sepulchral gloom / darkness — the specific grey-cold gloom of a burial chamber
  • Sepulchral atmosphere — a place that feels like you have entered a tomb
  • Sepulchral expression — a face that looks hollow, grave, and deathlike

"Sepulchral" is a formal, literary word. You will find it in novels, poems, essays, and dramatic speech — not in everyday casual conversation. When a writer reaches for this word, they are not just describing something dark; they are summoning a very deliberate, precise image. It carries weight. It has gravitas. It slows the reader down and makes them feel the cold stone and the silence.

Using it casually or overusing it weakens it. It is a word that earns its power by being deployed carefully, at the right moment, when nothing else will do.
A Final Image to Seal It

Imagine walking into an old stone crypt beneath a cathedral. The door swings shut behind you. The air is cold and perfectly still. There is no sound — not even the echo of your own footsteps carries far. The light from a narrow slit in the wall falls in a grey, weak beam. Stone coffins line the walls. The silence feels like a physical thing pressing against your ears.

That entire experience — the cold, the hollow stillness, the grey light, the nearness of death — is what "sepulchral" means.

When you call a voice sepulchral, you are saying it sounds like that crypt feels. When you call an atmosphere sepulchral, you are saying a place carries that exact quality. That is the word, in full.
14435:
A sequel is a work — such as a book, film, TV show, or video game — that continues the story of an earlier work. It picks up where the previous one left off and follows the same world, characters, or events forward in time.

Think of it like this: if the original work is a chapter, the sequel is the next chapter. The story is not over; it keeps going.

For something to be a sequel, two things must be true:

  1. It comes after the original work (in terms of story time — events in a sequel happen later than events in the original).
  2. It is connected to the original — same characters, same world, or a direct continuation of the same plot.

A completely separate, unrelated story is not a sequel, even if it is made by the same author or director.

• The Dark Knight (2008) is a sequel to Batman Begins (2005). The story of Bruce Wayne continues from where it stopped.
  • Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets is a sequel to Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone. Harry returns to Hogwarts, and the story moves forward.
  • Toy Story 2 is a sequel to Toy Story. Woody and Buzz are back, and new events unfold.

In each case, you can watch or read the sequel and witness what happens next.
An Important Nuance: Story Time vs. Release Time

The word sequel refers to the story's timeline, not necessarily when the work was published or released.

However, in almost all practical cases, a sequel is also released later than the original. You write the first book, then write the sequel. The sequel is published second because it comes second in the story.

This matters because it helps distinguish a sequel from a prequel (explained below).

Understanding what a sequel is not will sharpen your understanding greatly.

Not a remake. A remake retells the same story again, often with new actors or a new style. A sequel tells a new story that happens after the original.

Not a spin-off. A spin-off takes a character or element from the original and builds a separate, branching story around them — one that does not directly continue the main plot. For example, a TV show focused on a side character from a movie is a spin-off, not a sequel. A sequel stays close to the main storyline and moves it forward.

Not a prequel. A prequel is the opposite of a sequel. It tells the story of what happened before the original. So if a sequel answers "what happened next?", a prequel answers "what happened before all this?" Many people confuse these two, so keep this distinction sharp in your mind.
The Sequel's Relationship with the Original

A sequel depends on the original. This is one of its defining qualities. If you watch a sequel without having seen the original, you will likely feel lost — you won't know the characters, their history, or why certain things matter. The sequel assumes you already know the earlier story.

This is different from a standalone work, which is designed to be fully understood on its own with no prior knowledge required.
Can There Be More Than One Sequel?

Yes, absolutely. A story can have multiple sequels, one after another, each continuing forward:

  • Original → Sequel → Sequel to the Sequel → ...

When there are exactly three connected works, the whole set is called a trilogy. When there are many, the whole collection is often called a series or franchise.

Each individual follow-up in the chain is still called a sequel (though sometimes the second sequel is informally called a "threequel," but this is playful slang, not a formal term).
The Word in Broader, Non-Entertainment Contexts

While sequel is most commonly used in books, films, and games, it can also appear in more general or formal writing to mean any event or situation that follows and grows out of a previous one.

For example: "The economic collapse was the sequel to years of poor financial decisions."

Here, it means the collapse was the direct result or continuation of what came before — it grew out of it, just as a movie sequel grows out of its original film. This usage is less common in everyday speech but worth knowing.

A sequel is a follow-up work that continues the story of an earlier work by showing what happens next to the same characters or within the same world — and it assumes you are already familiar with the original.
14436:
A sequela is a medical condition or health problem that is the direct, lasting consequence of a previous disease, injury, or medical event.

In other words, it is not the original illness itself — it is the damage, disorder, or dysfunction that the original illness leaves behind or sets in motion.

Think of it this way: if a disease is a fire, the sequela is the smoke damage, the structural weakening, or the scarring that remains after the fire is put out.
The Most Important Thing to Understand

The word sequela captures a very specific relationship between two things:

Something bad happened first → and because of that, something else went wrong afterward.

The sequela is always the "because of that" part. It would not exist if the original event had never happened. That causal link — that the first event caused the second condition — is what makes something a sequela, not just a coincidence.

Because this word comes from Latin and is used in formal medical writing, its plural is not "sequelas" — it is sequelae. You will see this form very often in clinical and scientific texts, possibly more often than the singular.
Where You Will See This Word

Sequela (or sequelae) is used almost exclusively in medical, clinical, and scientific writing. Doctors, researchers, and medical students use it routinely. You will encounter it in:

  • Medical journals and research papers
  • Clinical case reports
  • Discharge summaries and hospital records
  • Public health documents
  • Neurology, infectious disease, and rehabilitation medicine especially

It is a precise, technical term. In everyday conversation, people would say "aftereffect," "long-term complication," or "lasting damage" instead. But in medicine, "sequela" is the single, exact word that carries this specific meaning efficiently.
Real-World Examples (This Is Where It Clicks)

Example 1 — Stroke

A person suffers a stroke. The stroke causes damage to part of the brain that controls movement. After the stroke is over, they are left with weakness or paralysis on one side of their body. That weakness is a sequela of the stroke. The stroke happened; the paralysis is what it left behind.

Example 2 — Meningitis

A child contracts bacterial meningitis (a dangerous brain infection). They recover and survive — but they are left with permanent hearing loss. The hearing loss is a sequela of the meningitis. The infection damaged the auditory nerves, and that damage persists even after the infection itself is gone.

Example 3 — COVID-19

A person recovers from a severe case of COVID-19, but months later they still experience extreme fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and shortness of breath. These persistent problems are sequelae of COVID-19 — what is commonly known as "Long COVID" in clinical circles.

Example 4 — Burn Injury

A person survives a serious burn. Once the wound heals, they are left with thick, tight scar tissue that restricts movement in their arm. That scarring and restricted movement are sequelae of the burn.

Example 5 — Polio (A Fascinating and Important Case)

Some people who contracted polio decades ago — and fully recovered at the time — later develop a new set of muscle weakness and fatigue in their 50s or 60s. This is called post-polio syndrome, and it is a late sequela of polio. The original infection had set off a slow process of nerve deterioration that only became apparent much later.

This last example introduces an important concept: sequelae do not always appear immediately. They can emerge years or even decades after the original event.
Key Distinctions — What Sequela Is NOT

Because several medical terms are easy to confuse with "sequela," it is worth drawing sharp lines between them.

Sequela vs. Symptom

A symptom is something you experience while you are sick — the fever, the pain, the rash, the cough. A sequela is what lingers or develops after the illness has ended or stabilized. Symptoms are during; sequelae are after.

Sequela vs. Complication

A complication is an additional problem that arises during the course of a disease or its treatment, often unexpectedly — for example, a surgical patient developing a blood clot during recovery. A sequela is specifically the downstream, lasting consequence that follows the original event. The boundary is not always perfectly rigid in practice, and some medical writers use the terms somewhat interchangeably, but the classic distinction is: complications happen alongside or during; sequelae follow after.

Sequela vs. Side Effect

A side effect is an unintended consequence of a treatment (like a medication causing nausea). A sequela is a consequence of the disease or injury itself, not of its treatment.

1. Sequelae can be temporary or permanent.
Some are short-lived — for example, muscle weakness after a prolonged illness that resolves with rehabilitation. Others are permanent, like the hearing loss from meningitis.

2. Sequelae can appear immediately or much later.
Some are obvious right after the original event. Others, like post-polio syndrome, are "late sequelae" — they develop after a delay of months, years, or decades.

3. Sequelae can be physical, neurological, or psychiatric.
A traumatic brain injury might leave someone with headaches (physical), memory problems (neurological), or depression (psychiatric). All of these can be called sequelae of the brain injury.

4. Sequelae can be mild or severe.
A mild sequela might be a faint scar. A severe sequela might be permanent paralysis or cognitive impairment.
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "The paralysis is a sequela of his stroke."
  • "Cognitive impairment is a well-documented sequela of untreated lead poisoning."
  • "Researchers are studying the neurological sequelae of COVID-19 infection."
  • "Post-traumatic stress disorder can be a psychological sequela of severe physical trauma."

If you want a single, reliable way to remember what this word means, hold onto this:

A sequela is the medical scar that one illness or injury leaves on your health — the condition that exists because of something that came before it.

It is not what is happening to you now during your illness. It is what your illness did to you — the lasting mark it made — that you carry after the illness itself is behind you.
14437:
A sequence is a group of things arranged in a specific order, where each item comes after the previous one, and where that order itself is meaningful. It is not just a random collection of things — it is items lined up in a chain, each one occupying a specific position: first, second, third, and so on.

Think of the alphabet: A, B, C, D, E. That is a sequence. Every letter has a fixed place, and the arrangement is intentional. If you jumble those letters randomly — D, B, A, E, C — you still have the same letters, but the sequence is gone. The word "sequence" is fundamentally about ORDER.

The reason "sequence" is such a precise and powerful word is that it tells you the arrangement itself carries meaning. In a sequence, switching items around changes everything.

Imagine a lock combination: 3 → 7 → 2 opens the lock. But 7 → 3 → 2, or 2 → 7 → 3, will not work — even though they contain the exact same numbers. The numbers alone are not enough. The sequence is what matters.

Or imagine a recipe: mix the batter, pour it into a pan, then bake it. If you bake the empty pan first and then pour in the batter, the sequence is broken — and so is the recipe. The steps are only meaningful in their correct order.
A Sequence Can Be Finite or Infinite

A sequence can be short and finite, meaning it has a definite start and a definite end. Your morning routine is a finite sequence: wake up → brush teeth → shower → eat breakfast. It ends.

A sequence can also be infinite, meaning it continues forever with no end. The sequence of whole numbers — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5... — is infinite. You can always add one more. In mathematics especially, infinite sequences are extremely common and important.
How "Sequence" Is Used in Different Areas

In Everyday Life

We encounter sequences constantly. A traffic light follows a sequence: red → green → yellow → back to red. A story has a sequence: beginning → middle → end. When you describe how an accident happened, you describe the sequence of events — what happened first, what happened next, and what happened last. The sequence tells the story.

In Mathematics

In math, a sequence is a list of numbers arranged in a specific order, usually following a rule or pattern. For example, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is a sequence where each number increases by 2. The sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 — where each number is the sum of the two before it — is the famous Fibonacci sequence. In math, the position of each number matters enormously. The "5th term" of a sequence and the "10th term" are precise, defined things — because the order is fixed.

In Film and Storytelling

In movies, a "sequence" refers to a connected group of scenes that form one unified, complete unit within the larger film. A "car chase sequence" is a series of scenes that depict a car chase, all flowing together as one coherent piece. An "opening sequence" is the group of scenes that begin a film. The scenes in a sequence belong together because they collectively tell one mini-story within the bigger story.

In Science and Biology

Scientists use this word constantly. A DNA sequence is the specific order of chemical building blocks along a strand of DNA. That order determines everything — what proteins an organism makes, what it looks like, how it functions. Change the sequence, even slightly, and you change the organism. The order is the information. This is why sequencing DNA is such a big deal in modern science.

In Music

In music theory, a sequence is when a melodic or harmonic phrase is repeated, but at a higher or lower pitch each time. The same shape of notes is played, just starting from a different point on the scale. It is the recognizable repetition of a pattern in a shifted position.

Sequence vs. Series: These two words are close cousins and often used interchangeably. The subtle difference is that "sequence" puts stronger emphasis on the strict ORDER of items, while "series" tends to focus more on the items themselves as a related group. A "series of unfortunate events" focuses on the events as a related collection. A "sequence of events" focuses on the order in which they happened.

Sequence vs. List: A list is simply a collection of items, and it may or may not be ordered. A grocery list, for example, doesn't care what order you buy things in. A sequence, by contrast, is always ordered — the position of each item is fixed and meaningful.

Sequence vs. Pattern: A pattern is a repeating design or structure. A sequence can contain a pattern (like 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3...), but it doesn't need to. A sequence simply needs to be ordered; a pattern needs repetition. All patterns involve sequences, but not all sequences are patterns.

"In sequence" means doing things in the correct, intended order. If a doctor says "take these three medications in sequence," they mean take the first, then the second, then the third — in that exact order, not all at once and not shuffled around.

"Out of sequence" means something appeared or happened in the wrong order. "The book's pages were printed out of sequence" means they came out in the wrong order — page 7 before page 4, for example.

"A sequence of events" simply means a series of things that happened one after another in time. This phrase is especially common when telling a story or explaining how something unfolded.

"The sequence of events" (with "the") is used when referring to a specific, known chain of happenings — for example, investigators trying to reconstruct "the sequence of events" in a crime means they are trying to figure out exactly what happened first, second, third, and so on.

No matter where you meet the word "sequence" — in math, biology, film, music, or everyday conversation — it always delivers the same core message: things arranged in a specific order, each item following the one before it, where the order itself is important and meaningful.

A sequence is not just "a bunch of things." It is "a bunch of things, each in their rightful place, forming a chain." Take the chain apart, scramble the links, and you no longer have that sequence — you have chaos.

Whenever you see or hear the word, ask yourself: what is the first thing, what comes next, and does the order matter? If the answer is yes, you are dealing with a sequence.
14438:
To sequester means to isolate or separate something (or someone) from the rest, and keep it apart — usually for a specific purpose or by force.

Think of it like this: imagine picking one apple out of a basket and placing it in a separate box, away from all the others. You have sequestered that apple. The key ideas baked into this word are:

  • Separation — something is removed from its usual environment or group.
  • Deliberateness — it doesn't happen by accident. Someone or something causes the separation.
  • A reason behind it — the isolation serves a goal (safety, fairness, control, storage, etc.)

The same core idea — deliberate isolation — shows up in several different areas of life. Here they all are:

1. Isolating a Person or Group (General Use)

You can sequester a person or a group of people by cutting them off from the outside world.

"The scientists were sequestered in a remote research station for six months."

Here, the scientists are separated from society and kept in one place. They can't freely come and go.

"She sequestered herself in her room to study for the exam."

Notice here she chose to isolate herself. You can sequester yourself, meaning you voluntarily withdraw from the world around you. This is a slightly softer, more poetic use of the word.

2. Sequestering a Jury (Legal Use — People)

This is one of the most common places you'll hear this word, especially in news about big court trials.

When a jury is sequestered, the jurors are kept completely isolated from the public, from the news, and from outside information for the entire duration of the trial. They may be housed in a hotel, cut off from their phones, TV, and newspapers.

Why? Because the law wants jurors to decide the case only based on what they hear inside the courtroom — not based on news headlines, public opinion, or conversations with friends and family. Sequestering them protects the fairness of the trial.

"The judge decided to sequester the jury because the case was attracting enormous media attention."

3. Seizing or Holding Assets (Legal Use — Property)

In law, to sequester can also mean to take hold of someone's property — money, assets, or belongings — and keep it under legal control until a dispute is resolved.

Think of it as the law saying: "We're locking this away so nobody can touch it until we figure out who it rightfully belongs to, or until the person pays what they owe."

"The court sequestered the company's funds while the fraud investigation was ongoing."

The money hasn't been permanently taken away — it's just frozen and separated from the owner's control for the time being.

4. Carbon Sequestration (Scientific Use)

This is a hugely important use of the word in environmental science.

To sequester carbon means to capture carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the atmosphere and store it somewhere so it can't continue warming the planet.

Nature does this naturally — trees and plants absorb CO₂ and lock it inside their wood, roots, and soil. Oceans do it too. Scientists are also developing technologies that artificially pull CO₂ out of the air and pump it deep underground for long-term storage.

"Planting more forests is one of the most effective ways to sequester carbon."

The carbon is being separated from the atmosphere and stored away — the same core idea as always, just applied to chemistry and climate.

5. Budget Sequestration (Political/Government Use)

In government and politics — particularly in the United States — sequestration refers to a process where a set of government funds is automatically cut off or withheld from spending.

It's as if the government puts a portion of its budget in a locked box and says, "This money cannot be spent." This usually happens as a result of a law that forces automatic spending cuts when politicians fail to agree on a budget.

"The sequester led to automatic cuts across nearly every government department."

Again, the same idea: money is isolated, separated, and made unavailable.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Sequester" is a formal word. You won't typically hear it in casual everyday conversation. It belongs more in legal documents, news reporting, scientific writing, and formal speeches.

It also carries a sense of authority and control — someone in power (a judge, the law, nature, a government) is doing the separating. Even when a person sequesters themselves, there's a sense of strong, deliberate will behind the action.

Compared to simpler words like "isolate" or "separate," sequester sounds more official, more purposeful, and often implies that the separation will last for a defined period and serve a very specific function.
How It Differs from Similar Words

IdeaWhy "Sequester" Is Different

Isolate is the closest synonym. But "isolate" is neutral and general — you can isolate almost anything for almost any reason. "Sequester" implies more formality, more specific purpose, and often some kind of authority or official process behind the action.

Confiscate means to permanently take something away, usually as a punishment. Sequestering property is different — it's temporary and neutral (the property may be returned).

Quarantine means isolating something to prevent the spread of disease. Sequestering is broader — it isn't limited to health situations.

Withdraw means to pull back. You can withdraw yourself, but it doesn't carry the sense of being kept apart that sequester does.

No matter the context — a jury, carbon dioxide, government money, or a person — "sequester" always means the same thing at its core:

To deliberately separate and keep something away from its usual surroundings, for a specific and purposeful reason.

The thing being sequestered is removed, held apart, and kept that way — whether by a judge, a law, a scientific process, or personal choice.

Once you internalize that central idea — deliberate separation with purpose — every use of this word, in any field, will immediately make sense to you.
14439:
Sequestration means the act of separating, isolating, or setting something aside — keeping it away from where it normally exists or belongs. Think of it as deliberately putting something "in a box" and locking it away from everything else.

This one concept — separation and isolation — runs through every use of this word. But depending on the context, it takes on different flavours. Here are all the major ways this word is used:

In its most basic sense, sequestration simply means the removal or isolation of something from its surroundings.

For example, if you took a group of people and locked them away in a hotel, completely cut off from the outside world, that act of isolating them is sequestration.

This is one of the most common uses of the word. In law, sequestration means the seizure or taking away of someone's property by a legal authority — usually a court or government — and holding it until a dispute is settled, a debt is paid, or a judgment is fulfilled.

Imagine you owe money to someone and refuse to pay. A court might step in and seize your assets (your property, money, or possessions) and hold them in a kind of legal lockbox. That forced removal and holding of your property is sequestration.

It can also refer to freezing someone's assets during an ongoing legal battle, so that neither side can touch the disputed property until the case is resolved.

Key ideas here:

  • Something is taken away from its owner.
  • It's held separately under official authority.
  • It's usually temporary, pending a legal outcome.

This meaning is especially common in the United States. Here, sequestration refers to automatic, across-the-board cuts in government spending, triggered by a law when the government fails to meet a budget target.

Think of it this way: the government sets a rule that says, "If we spend more than a certain amount, money will be automatically taken away from various departments — no exceptions, no negotiation." The mechanical, forced withholding of that money is called sequestration.

It's controversial because the cuts are blunt and automatic. They don't distinguish between important programs and less critical ones — they just slash across everything equally, like a lawnmower cutting everything to the same height regardless of what's growing.

The United States famously went through a sequestration in 2013, when around $85 billion in automatic cuts hit the federal budget, affecting defence, education, healthcare, and more.

Key ideas here:

  • Money is withheld from government departments.
  • The cuts are automatic and mandated by law.
  • They happen when a spending limit is breached.

This is the most widely discussed scientific use today. Carbon sequestration is the process by which carbon dioxide (CO₂) is captured from the atmosphere and stored somewhere so it doesn't contribute to climate change.

Nature does this on its own — trees absorb CO₂ and store the carbon in their wood and roots; oceans absorb huge amounts of CO₂ from the air; soil also traps carbon. This is called natural sequestration.

Humans are also developing technology to artificially pull CO₂ out of the air or catch it at the source (like at a factory chimney) and pump it deep underground into rock formations where it stays trapped. This is called carbon capture and storage, or artificial/technological sequestration.

Key ideas here:

  • Carbon (CO₂) is separated from the atmosphere.
  • It is stored somewhere it can't cause harm.
  • The goal is to fight global warming.

In high-profile criminal trials, a judge may order jury sequestration — meaning the jury members are isolated from the public for the duration of the trial. They may be housed in a hotel, have their phone and internet access restricted, and be prevented from reading news or talking to family and friends about the case.

The purpose is to protect the fairness of the trial — to make sure jurors make their decision based only on evidence presented in court, not on outside influences like media coverage or public pressure.

This is perhaps the closest to the word's most literal meaning: physically separating a group of people from the rest of the world.

In chemistry, sequestration refers to binding or isolating specific ions (charged particles) in a solution so they become inactive or are removed from a reaction. This is done using certain chemical agents called sequestering agents or chelating agents.

For example, if you have unwanted metal ions in water that are causing problems (like interfering with soap or causing staining), you add a chemical that "grabs" those ions and locks them away so they can't cause trouble anymore. That locking-away process is sequestration.

This meaning is mostly encountered in industrial chemistry, water treatment, and food science (where sequestering agents are used as food additives to preserve colour and texture).

Here's a simple mental map to remember all of this:

Sequestration always means: something is separated, isolated, or locked away from where it normally is — usually deliberately, and usually for a specific purpose.

Government budgetMoneyTo enforce spending limits by law
EnvironmentalCarbon dioxideTo reduce climate change

Sequestration is the noun for the act of taking something — property, money, carbon, people, particles — and deliberately separating it, isolating it, or locking it away from the rest, usually under some authority, rule of law, or natural/technological process.
